topic: software supply chain security; evidence calibration
status: bounded cross-paper synthesis; not a prevalence estimate or novelty claim
claim: The sampled literature labels different evidence stages as security outcomes: news-reported incidents, human-coded intent/impact, code-pattern/PR heuristics, suspicious-package detections, maintainer-confirmed malware, and model-metadata mismatches. These labels cannot be pooled as one measure of attack prevalence or risk. The next study should preserve the evidence level and quantify uncertainty when moving from signal to confirmed malicious artifact, reachability, and downstream impact.
positive_evidence: The 2023 LLM study's GPT accuracy varies from 52% on impacts to 88% on intent; manual agreement for impacts is only κ=0.34.
The 2023 npm study flags 12,465 PRs using six regex-based features but explicitly says the method does not establish that flagged updates are malicious.
The previously audited MALOSS paper reports 339 newly suspicious packages, of which maintainers confirmed/removed 278, making confirmation a distinct downstream stage.
The PTM naming study identifies metadata inconsistencies, but its labels do not establish artifact provenance, malicious behavior, or task performance.
counterevidence: MALOSS demonstrates that automated screening can surface candidates that are later confirmed by maintainers; staged triage is operationally useful.
The flagged npm changes may represent legitimate runtime behaviors and still be useful risk signals even when not confirmed malicious.
The LLM study finds high intent accuracy where human annotators agree, so automated assistance may work for well-supported dimensions.

sources.sections: MALOSS pipeline, manual verification, and limits

falsifiable_test: Construct a two-ecosystem corpus and independently adjudicate a blinded stratified sample at five levels: heuristic signal, human-reviewed suspicious behavior, confirmed malicious artifact, vulnerable/reachable code, and observed downstream impact. Report precision/recall and inter-rater agreement at each transition; test whether source-citing LLM triage improves speed without reducing calibration or abstention quality. The lead weakens if the stages are highly predictive of one another and reviewer agreement is high across dimensions.
limitations: One six-paper heterogeneous cell plus targeted follow-up; no systematic attack-corpus audit. The 2023 PR heuristic remains a potentially useful risk signal, even though it is not ground truth.

topic: AI/software supply chain; model artifact provenance and validation
status: bounded research lead; broad gap claim rejected
claim: Pre-trained model packages carry reuse-relevant semantics across names, config, architecture, weights, data, and task, but a classifier trained on architecture features is strong for broad model type and materially weaker for fine-grained architecture/task labels. Later developer-reported studies find model- and data-level security concerns, while a current research agenda identifies unresolved cross-ecosystem and exploitability measurement. This motivates artifact-aware assurance, but does not establish that model registries are unsafe or that existing naming checks prevent attacks.
positive_evidence: The sampled PTM study combines 108-user survey evidence with mining of 14,296 popular model packages and finds users consult model cards/config and sometimes inspect/run models to check names.

DARA's body/table reports up to 99% model_type accuracy while its abstract reports 94%; architecture is 72%, and task top-1 accuracy is 72.3% in Table 14 versus approximately 76.3% in narrative. Task top-1 F1 is 56.5%. The exact v3 has an additional time boundary: it was revised in 2025 and its study data run through 2024.

A 2025 developer-discussion study classifies 753 sampled posts into 32 issue and 24 solution categories across system/software, tools/ecosystem, model, and data; some model/data issues lack concrete solutions.

A 2026 research agenda identifies cross-ecosystem measurement and real-world exploitability of transitive vulnerabilities as unresolved, and proposes studying dependency patterns introduced by AI-generated code.
counterevidence: The PTM paper presents DARA as a proof of concept and demonstrates strong broad model-type classification, so some metadata validation is already feasible.
The 2025 thematic post sample and 2026 agenda are not prevalence estimates or completed cross-ecosystem experiments.
DARA's dataset is specific to Hugging Face and uses shuffled 5-fold evaluation; performance on unseen architectures, other registries, and malicious artifacts is unestablished.

falsifiable_test: Build a held-out-by-architecture and held-out-by-time benchmark across two model registries. Compare name-only, config-only, architecture/weights, signed provenance, and combined checks for metadata accuracy, model/task mismatch, artifact provenance, and downstream behavior. Include open-world labels and report class-specific calibration. The lead weakens if name/architecture signals alone robustly predict provenance and runtime behavior across registries and time.
limitations: Current agenda evidence is prospective, and the 2025 post study is thematic. No direct malicious PTM artifact evaluation was performed. The 2023 DARA model does not test security or provenance.
